e.etymology: An English spelling of the Welsh name Rhys (ardor), long used as a surname. Its use for girls is American and dates from the 1980s onward.

assoc.t: Reese's Peanut Butter Cups candy
actress Reese Witherspoon

e.meaning: mythical bird reborn from its own ashes
e.etymology: From Greek phoinix by way of Latin, the name of the mythical bird that burns and rises again from its ashes, a symbol of renewal. A modern given name for boys and girls.

assoc.t: Phoenix, capital of Arizona
mythical firebird that rises from its ashes
Phoenix, Jean Grey's cosmic alter ego in X-Men

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English campas (enclosure) plus denu (valley). A modern choice as a first name.

assoc.t: Camden, New Jersey, across the river from Philadelphia
Camden Yards, the Baltimore Orioles ballpark
Camden Town, London market district

e.etymology: An English form of Zachariah and Zacharias, from Hebrew Zekharyah (Yahweh has remembered), the name of several biblical figures including the father of John the Baptist.
namesakes: Zachary Quinto (actor, Spock in the Star Trek films)

e.meaning: from the Roman family name Antonius, of unknown meaning
e.etymology: The Italian and Spanish form of Anthony, from the Roman family name Antonius, which is probably Etruscan and of unknown meaning.
namesakes: Antonio Vivaldi (composer of The Four Seasons)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Ester, the Persian queen of the biblical Book of Esther. It is usually linked to an Old Persian word for star, or else to the goddess Ishtar.
namesakes: Queen Esther (biblical queen who saved her people)
Esther Williams (swimmer and MGM film star)

assoc.t: Book of Esther in the Bible, read at Purim

e.etymology: A 2020s respelling of Ailani, a modern name modeled on Hawaiian names that end in lani (sky, heaven), such as Leilani. It rose quickly in the United States, mostly in Hispanic families.
From Italian Alina or a Latinate form of French Aline, both pet forms of Germanic Adela and Adeline (noble). It is common across central and eastern Europe.
The Spanish and Italian form of Emil, from the Roman family name Aemilius, traditionally tied to Latin aemulus (rival).
From Hebrew Immanu'el (God is with us), the name given in Isaiah's prophecy and applied to Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew.

assoc.t: biblical title for Christ, as in O Come, O Come, Emmanuel

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Catherine, from Greek Aikaterine. The meaning pure comes from a later link to Greek katharos.

assoc.t: Santa Catalina Island off Southern California
Catalina dressing, the sweet red salad dressing
the Catalina Wine Mixer joke from the film Step Brothers

e.etymology: The Spanish and Nordic form of Matthias, from Greek Matthias and Hebrew Mattityahu (gift of Yahweh). In the New Testament Matthias is the apostle chosen to replace Judas.

e.meaning: uncertain; often given as little rock or handsome
e.etymology: From Old Breton Alan, borne by early Breton saints and brought to England by the Normans. Its origin and meaning are disputed.
namesakes: Alan Turing (computer science pioneer and codebreaker)
Alan Rickman (actor, Snape in Harry Potter)

e.etymology: From the flowering tree, which was named in the 1700s for French botanist Pierre Magnol. One of the flower names taken up as girls' names in the 19th century.

assoc.t: Magnolia, Chip and Joanna Gaines's home and TV brand
Magnolia, the 1999 Paul Thomas Anderson film
Magnolia Bakery, New York bakery known for banana pudding

e.etymology: A modern American form of Adeline with the -lynn ending, also read as Ada plus Lynn. Adeline goes back to Germanic adal (noble).
A respelling of Emerson, an English surname meaning son of Emery. Emery is a Norman name of Germanic origin whose second element means ruler.

assoc.t: essayist Ralph Waldo Emerson, by sound

e.etymology: From an English surname taken from Rimington in northern England: Old English rima (edge, border) plus -ing and tun (settlement).
namesakes: Remington Steele (1980s TV detective played by Pierce Brosnan)
Frederic Remington (painter and sculptor of the Old West)

assoc.t: Remington rifles, shotguns and ammunition
Remington electric shavers and hair tools
Remington Steele, 1980s TV detective
Frederic Remington, artist of the Old West

e.note: Best known as a gun brand. Some parents pick it for that reason and others avoid it.

e.meaning: gift, by tradition; the Hebrew is uncertain
e.etymology: From Hebrew Yishai through Greek and Latin. In the Bible Jesse is the father of King David. The name came into English use after the Protestant Reformation.

assoc.t: Jesse James, Wild West outlaw

e.meaning: hedged enclosure; also descendant of Aodh (fire)
e.etymology: From a surname with two sources: English place names from Old English words for brushwood or an enclosure, and Irish Ó hAodha, descendant of Aodh (fire).
namesakes: Isaac Hayes (soul musician, Theme from Shaft)

assoc.t: Rutherford B. Hayes, nineteenth US president

e.etymology: From Latin felix (happy, lucky, fruitful), a Roman byname taken up by early Christians and borne by many saints and several popes.
namesakes: Felix Unger (the neat one in The Odd Couple)

assoc.t: Felix the Cat, black-and-white cartoon cat

e.etymology: A spelling of Caden, a name invented by American parents in the 1990s to rhyme with Aidan, Braden, Hayden and Jayden. This spelling can also be read as Kai plus -den.

e.meaning: son of Madoc, a Welsh name meaning fortunate
e.etymology: From a Welsh surname meaning son of Madog or Madoc, from mad (fortunate, good). It took off in the US after Angelina Jolie named her son Maddox in 2002.

assoc.t: Maddox Jolie-Pitt, eldest son of Angelina Jolie

e.etymology: From French Valérie and Latin Valeria, feminine of the Roman family name Valerius, from valere (to be strong).

assoc.t: Valerie, the song made famous by Amy Winehouse

e.etymology: From the Irish surname Ó Sluaghadháin, descendant of Sluaghadhán, a pet form of a name meaning expedition or raid.
namesakes: Sloane Peterson (Ferris's girlfriend in Ferris Bueller's Day Off)

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English aesc (ash tree) plus leah (wood, clearing). Once a boys' name, it became a leading American girls' name in the 1980s.
namesakes: Ashley Wilkes (Gone with the Wind character)

assoc.t: Ashley Furniture, home furnishings chain

e.etymology: From an English surname and Norfolk place name, the Old English personal name Becca plus ham (homestead). Its use as a first name follows soccer star David Beckham.

assoc.t: David Beckham, English soccer star

e.etymology: The French and Spanish form of Nicholas, from Greek Nikolaos: nike (victory) plus laos (people). Saint Nicholas of Myra spread the name across Europe.
An American spelling of Aidan, the name of an Irish saint, from Irish Aodhán, a pet form of Aodh (fire).
The French form of Isabel, a medieval Spanish form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva (my God is an oath).

assoc.t: Isabelle, the cheerful assistant in Animal Crossing

e.etymology: A French pet form of Julie, from Latin Julia, feminine of the Roman family name Julius. The root is uncertain; the reading youthful is traditional.
namesakes: Juliette Gordon Low (founder of the Girl Scouts)

assoc.t: Juliet of Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet

e.etymology: From the English word for the warmest season. It came into use as a girls' name around 1970 along with other nature and season names.
namesakes: Summer Smith (the sister in Rick and Morty)
Summer Sanders (Olympic swimmer and TV host)

e.meaning: from a surname probably meaning quarrelsome
e.etymology: From an English and Irish surname of Anglo-Norman origin with several sources, among them Middle English Baraud (quarrelsome) and Old French barat (trickery).
namesakes: Syd Barrett (founding member of Pink Floyd)

assoc.t: Barrett, maker of .50 caliber rifles
